text: When an agent edit rewrote the whole week instead of one day, the fix was architectural rather than a one-off patch. The client sends a snapshot of the active plan, or the staged proposal it is replying to, with each request, and the coach prompt is hardened for 'surgical preservation'. After that change, adding a core finisher or swapping Thursday and Friday changed only the targeted items.

The coach should pick its response format by intent. A plain question ('what is hypertrophy') should get a text answer with no card, a single-day edit should get a day card, and a weekly plan should get a week card. The day card had to be added because returning the full week for a one-day change was confusing.

A Modify button attaches the current proposal as a context chip. Free-typed requests without that chip generated a brand-new plan, and the chip should clear on send by calling the same function as the chip's close (x) control, so the logic isn't reimplemented.

text: Run a spec through a three-step check before handing it to a coding agent: LLM rewording, formalization into SMT-LIB formulas, and a satisfiability solver that flags rules that cannot simultaneously hold (e.g. 'place as back order' vs 'no order shall be back order').

facts: 7 to 10 sampled translations per requirement
clustering by logical equivalence
text: Detect ambiguity by sampling the LLM's formal translation of a sentence 7–10 times and clustering the results by logical equivalence; multiple clusters indicate the sentence has more than one meaning.
Classify spec defects into three types: ambiguity within a sentence (e.g. 'remove the record'), conflicts between rules, and gaps where no rule covers a state (e.g. an idle order).

When ambiguity is found, present the human with concrete alternative interpretations (e.g. delete the record vs retain but hide from users) and abstain or fall back to an LLM judge if no answer is given.

facts: 20–40% accuracy drop with unclear prompts

text: The speaker cites research claiming unclear prompts cause a 20–40% drop in code accuracy, that 60–90% of 'valid' code is still wrong, and roughly 2x more regressions on deploy.
Formal verification cannot be the oracle for spec correctness; the user must remain the final authority because of implicit domain knowledge, and evidence for formalization in agents is still thin.

Local, interactive, one-at-a-time prompting caps agent throughput at human speed. Per-developer setups (own models, skills, MCPs) also make cost efficiency, security and governance hard to manage centrally.

text: Write evals as critical user journeys phrased the way a user asks (e.g. 'Show me my top customers'), not as instructions to call a specific tool. Because every agent accepts natural language, the same eval set can compare harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex.

facts: Harbor eval framework supports only single user turn per the speakers
text: True multi-turn evals need a simulated user. An LLM follows a 'plan prompt' playbook to answer the agent's clarifying questions (e.g. which region), so you can check that the agent asked the right questions as well as whether it reached the goal. Frameworks like Harbor only support a single user turn.

Grade the path and the outcome, not the agent's final sentence. Check that the expected tools were called, in order, without unnecessary extra calls, and verify the real cloud resource state (region, availability, schema) matches what is expected.

Prefer deterministic scoring, such as running the golden query and comparing the data, and checking tool parameters. For the remainder, use checkbox-style LLM-judge scorecards and recalibrate them against human raters.

facts: Claude Code tool search / deferred tool loading
Large MCP tool schemas can cost thousands of tokens upfront
text: Harness token optimizations can silently hurt tool and skill selection. When Claude Code rolled out tool search, it changed how the team built tools. Some harnesses also truncate or drop skill descriptions when there are many skills, which only evals reveal.

Run ablation evals with each skill on vs off (same model, harness and CUJs) and plot goal completion against token cost. Keep skills that win on both or that substantially raise completion (e.g. a migration runbook), and retire old skills that add tokens without moving completion.

facts: MCP tasks return a task ID and the harness monitors them
Google Cloud has 50+ managed MCP servers

Their evals showed MCP tasks are the better fit: the call returns a task ID and the harness waits for a notification at no model cost.

<1% accuracy gain from full access
text: Citing an Anthropic blog post, the speaker says giving agents access to everything (all tables, all dbt files) raised accuracy by less than 1% while greatly increasing time spent, so context should be curated rather than exhaustive.

Each saved dataset is exposed to agents as a simple Markdown-like card with description, dependencies (lineage) and schema; the speaker calls lineage a must-have for agents, saying without it they 'hallucinate badly'.

facts: Presets shown for coach chat: welcome, with context, day proposal, week proposal, AI thinking
Avoids repeated Gemini API calls and token waste
text: Build a dev-only inspector route per component that renders it standalone with dummy data and one-click presets (welcome, thinking, day/week proposal, error). This lets you check AI-dependent UI states without replaying multi-step flows or calling the model each time.
Split the inspector's state panel into three groups: editable state, state from props (both changeable) and computed state (read-only). This shows how data flows from parent components.
List the component's tests in plain English on the inspector page and wire them both ways: clicking a test sets up the component for that case, and changing state highlights which tests are active.

Separate update skill for existing inspector pages
Took three attempts: AI Studio proof of concept, a failed big upfront Gemini web app prompt, then incremental work in Antigravity
text: Refine the inspector on one component first (the 'current set card'), then ask the agent to turn the finished result into a reusable skill ('component Inspector generator') plus a second skill for updating an existing inspector page. A new inspector for another card was then generated from one prompt in about seven minutes.

facts: Rule was first a global toggle and was changed to be scoped per session
A 'last updated' chip shows when the inspector page was last regenerated
Inspector mode is turned on and off with natural language
text: The inspector UI is generated statically from the code file, so it goes stale. Rather than live code introspection, the author added a session-scoped 'Inspector mode' rule, so while the mode is on the agent updates the component and its inspector page in the same request.

facts: Error presets: connection error, 500 error, simulate timeout

MCP: 6x cost, 5x time on hardest tasks
correctness: tie

text: In Arize's GitHub-repo management eval, MCP and CLI tied on correctness, but on the hardest tasks MCP cost about 6x more and took about 5x longer; MCP still wins for consumer/enterprise use because OAuth lets users grant access via a friendly browser prompt and admins control access.

facts: pass@k vs pass^k
example: 20% failure rate means 20% of customers get wrong answers
text: Use pass@k (succeeds at least once in k tries) for coding-style agents and pass^k (succeeds every time) for customer-facing agents like support; demos are pass@k, production is pass^k.

facts: capability eval target ~50%
regression eval target 100%
text: Split evals into capability evals (target ~50% pass rate as a hill to climb) and regression evals (expected 100%); graduate capability evals into the regression suite as the agent matures.

facts: Claude prefers XML tags
1-10 scores tend to return 7
binary + N/A output recommended
text: Effective LLM-judge prompts have five parts: a role, explicit good/bad criteria derived from reading traces, data clearly delimited (XML tags for Claude), labeled examples (test with and without to detect overfitting), and a constrained binary answer plus optional N/A rather than 1-10 scores, which cluster at 7.

facts: Arize agent 'Alex' called same tool 43 times in one run
check database state, e.g. refund actually created
text: Grade the outcome and actual system state rather than the agent's claimed path, but also inspect trajectories: Arize's agent Alex once called the same tool 43 times in one run while every span reported fine.

Arize AX ships agent-as-a-judge
judges prefer longer, confident, own-model outputs
text: Agent-as-a-judge outperforms plain LLM-as-a-judge: a Meta and KAUST paper found ~90% agreement with expert consensus vs ~70% for an LLM judge; judges should be calibrated against a human golden dataset and cross-provider to avoid self-preference, length and confidence bias.

Measuring impact remains the least mature area. Some clients are experimenting with using AI to score the value and intent of work so they can direct tokens and resources to the highest-value items.

text: The managed server uses OAuth with standard Looker SSO in a browser window, so no API keys or credentials are stored locally. Clients such as the VS Code Looker extension must first be registered by an admin.
Choosing between the two shifts governance ownership. With the managed server, Looker admins flip switches in a UI. With Toolbox, development teams own config files and server infrastructure.

facts: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) graph workflows
ADK human-in-the-loop via tool confirmation
text: Telling a single agent in its instructions to wait for human approval does not guarantee it will wait; a deterministic workflow node that pauses execution is needed to enforce human-in-the-loop review.

Model workflows as nodes (a function, an AI agent, or a wait-for-human step) and edges (dependencies and routing paths); common patterns are parallel, routing, trees (parent/child agents) and loops, and real apps combine them.

facts: Google ADK
text: In the refund demo, three checks (order, payment, refund history) run in parallel, join at a rules node, which routes the case to human review; after approval with a reason, a response agent drafts the reply using the facts plus the human decision.

text: Vector RAG can return a matching record that lacks facts the task needs; GraphRAG starts from a relevant record and follows relationships (order→payment, order→customer→refund history summary) to assemble complete context.

facts: BigQuery Graph
GQL (graph query language)
text: BigQuery Graph lets you define graph relationships over existing BigQuery tables and query connected records with GQL (graph query language); the same facts could be fetched with table joins, but defined relationships make multi-hop queries easier.

Both graph types carry trade-offs: workflow graphs take work to build and maintain (a few functions or one agent with tools may suffice for small tasks), and traversing more connections adds latency, cost and irrelevant info, so measure separate parallel reads versus one combined query in production.

Reliability is framed as 'Einstein 95% of the time, Mr. Bean 5%': if you can't tell which output is which, you can't automate, so narrow, extremely reliable intelligence beats occasional brilliance that must be verified.

facts: Claim from RLHF/InstructGPT work: GPT-2 sized model with RLHF vs. GPT-7 to 9 equivalent pretraining on instruction following
text: The 'bitterest lesson' is choosing the right training task: the RLHF paper showed a GPT-2-sized model with instruction-following training matched what would need roughly 'GPT-7 to 9' scale pretraining alone.

Treat LLM calls as a fourth 'semantic logic gate' embedded in software's inner loop (e.g., 'is this a real-looking Gmail address' instead of a regex) rather than a chatbot to the side that can't make costly decisions.

Agent designs are constrained by the 'tyranny of the KV cache': shared state across parallel sub-agents, non-O(N) memory via map-reduce over history, and smarter sub-agent routing are open problems because they fight KV cache efficiency.

facts: References an OpenAI / Hugging Face sandbox incident

Slop stems from unreliability: since AI can't be trusted with decisions that cost the operator, its costs get externalized onto recipients; reliable models could curb things like 'inbound hell'.

text: Replacing a general LLM judge with a few typed yes/no questions answered from tool 'receipts' sharply improved agent-output checking. ZoomInfo's LLM judge was right only 65% of the time and accepted fabricated success reports; a decision model with 7 questions caught 623 versus 294 failed-tool steps, while running 10x faster and 40x cheaper.

text: Production incidents drove specific spec mitigations: per-client consent against confused-deputy attacks, a ban on token passthrough, and validation of both token audience and issuer to block mix-up attacks.

facts: Examples cited: Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, ServiceNow agents, Sierra Agent Studio, Muse, Dots, Claude Duet, Figure
text: Agentic use cases fall into five archetypes: software engineering, enterprise automation, scientific/financial research, personal assistants and robotics. Personal assistants and robotics are hybrid edge-cloud deployments, while the first three are mostly cloud.

An agent is defined as an LLM in a harness with four design patterns: tool use, reasoning/planning, multi-agent orchestration and state/memory across sessions. Moving from stateless chat calls to stateful agents shifts bottlenecks to context management, orchestration and the tool-execution fabric (sandboxes, containers, tool latency).

Tooling and orchestration run primarily on CPUs, while reasoning and planning are split between CPU and accelerator. Infrastructure therefore needs dense CPUs that run many concurrent agents in isolated micro-VMs without noisy-neighbor issues, plus head-node CPUs that keep accelerators fully utilized.

facts: AI writes ~75% of Google's new code, up from <25% a few years ago
100,000 engineers use Antigravity daily
Gemini 3 era: launches every 2-3 months; now six releases in 16 weeks
text: Release speed comes from serving post-training candidates to 100,000+ Google engineers via blind battles and silent routing to experimental models, feeding failures back as new training tasks.

facts: Raw Live API, Google ADK or a custom wrapper change the code path but not the design decision
text: Classify every agent input as continuous (mic, live camera) or complete (screenshot, product photo, typed instruction). Stream what keeps changing and send a single complete item when one is enough. This decision holds whether you use raw Live, ADK or your own wrapper.

Slow work must never stall a live loop. Acknowledge immediately and move page loads, long tools, memory extraction and generation jobs off the hot path, then bring results back in on the next event such as a snapshot or memory read.

facts: Hybrid memory: SQL for facts, vectors for semantic understanding
text: Split agent memory into exact facts stored as structured data (SQL) and meaning/understanding stored in semantic vector memory. Long memory work runs in the background, off the live path.
Live video for agents is not an MP4 but still image frames sent over time. Use a snapshot when the agent needs to look and stream frames when it needs to watch.

facts: Google ADK: agent / runner / session structure
text: Google ADK separates concerns into three parts: the agent decides behavior, the runner runs it, and the session holds state. You describe the agent and ADK runs the live loop.

facts: Real Chrome window used for browser control

text: There are two delegation modes. Client delegation sends delegation events (with an ID and timestamp) to your own harness, including cascaded STT→agent→TTS stacks. Responses delegation lets OpenAI run a model from the Responses API with function tools and hosted tools such as web search and image generation.
